claims.claim: The work is anonymous; modern scholars believe it was written by an anonymous author who was not Clement of Rome.
The work was written around AD 120–140.
The work is actually a sermon or homily, not a letter.
The sermon focuses on self-control, repentance, and judgment.
The preacher addresses his audience as 'brothers and sisters.'
The work was traditionally believed to have been an epistle to the Christian Church in Corinth written by Clement of Rome in the late 1st century.
Eusebius, a 4th-century bishop, expressed doubt about the authenticity of a second epistle of Clement, stating there was only one recognized epistle.
Jerome in the 5th century also expressed similar doubts about the authenticity of a second epistle.
The work survives in the biblical Codex Alexandrinus (late 4th century) and the later Jerusalem Codex (1056), as well as in the Syriac version.
The work was included in some Bibles such as the Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Hierosolymitanus.
It is not included in the modern New Testament by active churches and is classified as New Testament apocrypha.
It is part of the Apostolic Fathers collection.
